title: Organisational Gender Pay Gaps in the UK: What Happened Post-Transparency?
journal: The B.E. Journal of Economic Analysis & Policy
abstract: Abstract Since April 2017 UK employers with over 250 employees have been required to publicly report their gender pay gap each year. We exploit this novel source of panel data on employer-level gender pay gaps to explore the factors associated with changing organisational gender pay gaps in the period immediately following transparency. Consistent with information, reflection and pressure brought by the legislation, we find greater narrowing of gender pay gaps in organisations with a larger absolute and relative initial gender pay gap. The latter is consistent with transparency per se providing a channel through which the impact of the legislation operates.

title: ‘Doing history teaching with GenAI’: an exploration of teaching practices during an AI pilot project in Germany
abstract: Although teachers’ actions are considered central to history lessons, little is known about their teaching practices with regard to the use of generative artificial intelligence. In this article, we ask which teaching practices were carried out among teachers in history lessons while using generative artificial intelligence in a pilot project at German schools with schulKI (schoolAI). To this end, we analysed interviews with and project documentation from 12 history teachers who took part in the pilot project. Based on considerations from practice theory and a socio-cultural view of history education, we analysed our data sources and identified four central teaching practices that characterise ‘doing history teaching with GenAI’: (a) obtaining support from generative artificial intelligence for the preparation of history lessons; (b) introducing practices of utilising generative artificial intelligence in history lessons; (c) integrating generative artificial intelligence into the implementation of history lessons; and (d) managing with situational demands through the use of generative artificial intelligence in history lessons. In this article, we present our praxeological observations and their socio-cultural interpretation in the field of tension between covering the curriculum and maintaining control in more detail. Finally, we discuss these against the background of the current state of research and draw conclusions for research and teaching practice.

title: What makes you trust digital data wallets? Antecedents of trust formation
abstract: Purpose Digital data wallets are emerging privacy-enhancing technologies that give users greater control over their personal information, yet trust remains a major barrier to adoption. This study aims to identify the factors shaping trust and how perceived risks moderate these relationships. Design/methodology/approach Using a mixed-methods approach, thirty qualitative interviews conducted in Austria, Romania and Spain identified four key antecedents of trust: trust in the Internet, trust in the community of internet users, trust in the provider and trust in the information system. A follow-up survey of 1,200 respondents tested the impact of these antecedents and the moderating role of perceived risks (identity theft and financial loss) on trust formation. Findings Results show that all antecedents, specifically performance expectancy, transparency, social influence and safety, significantly related to their respective trust targets, and that trust relationships are interdependent across targets. Risk perceptions strengthen the influence of performance expectancy and social influence but weaken the effect of transparency. Originality/value The study contributes to research on trust in digital data wallets by empirically applying and extending the application network-of-trust model to the context of decentralized personal data management. The findings demonstrate that the trust formation is differentiated across multiple trust targets and shaped by context-specific antecedents and perceived risks. The study also provides actionable insights for designers and policymakers seeking to build trustworthy digital data wallets.

title: Transposable element-host genome evolutionary arms race revealed by multi-modal epigenomic profiling in a telomere-to-telomere human genome reference
abstract: Abstract For a quarter of a century, transposable elements (TEs) have been recognized as a major component of the human genome, key drivers of regulatory innovation and participants in an ongoing evolutionary arms race with host defence systems. Using the newly released telomere-to-telomere ENCODE dataset, I quantified the epigenetic impact of 3.7 million TEs across evolutionary time by analysing seven epigenomic modalities in twelve human cell lines. I show that SINE-VNTR(Variable Number of Tandem Repeats)-Alu element (SVA) elements exhibit the strongest signatures of the arms race, progressively escaping H3K9me3-mediated heterochromatinization while acquiring CCCTC-binding factor (CTCF) and enhancer chromatin marks. Among Alu elements, the AluYb8 and AluYb9 subfamilies are accumulating CTCF binding, while seven long terminal repeats (LTR) subfamilies (human endogeneous retrovirus 16 intact copy (HERV16-int), MER11C, LTR43-int, HERVE-int, LTR22C, LTR5_Hs and HERVIP10FH-int) demonstrate arms race dynamics, acquiring active and H3K9me3-enriched contexts alongside CTCF binding. I further evaluated the contribution of epigenomic modalities to the host-transposable element conflict and found that transposon-driven evolution is dominated by evasion of host-imposed heterochromatinization primarily at H3K9me3 and secondarily at H3K27me3, together with progressive invasion into CTCF-rich regions. Enhancer, promoter and H3K36me3 marks appear to play limited roles. Collectively, these findings deepen our insight into the coevolutionary epigenomic dynamics between the human genome and TEs, and their associated regulatory innovation.

title: The policy relevance of climate-change scenarios for biodiversity research
The endometrium heals without fibrosis after menstruation: implications for uterine healing after cesarean delivery
abstract: Abstract Background The human endometrium undergoes repeated cycles of bleeding, inflammation, tissue breakdown, and repair. Unlike most adult tissues, which heal through fibrosis, the endometrium restores its architecture and function after menstruation without scar formation. This capacity for scarless repair is essential for implantation, placentation, and reproductive success. Content Cesarean delivery creates a deep surgical injury that heals with fibrosis, altered extracellular matrix organization, and abnormal tissue architecture. Cesarean scar defects, cesarean scar pregnancy, and placenta accreta spectrum arise preferentially within these regions of abnormal healing. We examine the possibility that menstruation provides a physiologic model for understanding how the uterus restores tissue architecture without fibrosis. Summary The contrast between menstrual repair and post-cesarean healing raises a fundamental question: why does one form of uterine injury restore normal architecture while another leads to scar formation? Current discussions of cesarean closure focus largely on mechanical outcomes such as scar thickness and uterine rupture, whereas the biologic determinants of uterine healing remain poorly understood. Outlook A deeper understanding of the mechanisms that permit scarless repair of the endometrium may provide new opportunities to improve uterine healing after cesarean delivery and reduce the burden of infertility, adenomyosis, cesarean scar pregnancy, and placenta accreta spectrum.

title: Part-time farming and cultivated land quality protection among large-scale farmers: a U-shaped relationship—evidence from China
abstract: Introduction Promoting farmers’ adoption of cultivated land quality protection practices is essential for long-term food security. This study develops a decision-making framework to examine how part-time farming affects the land protection behavior of large-scale farmers through three key production factors: land, capital, and labor. Methods Using survey data from 532 large-scale farming households in Jiangxi Province, China, this study applies ordinary least squares (OLS) and two-stage least squares (2SLS) models to estimate the linear and nonlinear effects of part-time farming on cultivated land quality protection practices. It further investigates the underlying mechanisms and examines heterogeneity by off-farm employment duration, exposure to natural disasters, geographical location, and dependence on rice income. Results and discussion The results reveal a significant U-shaped relationship between the degree of part-time farming and cultivated land quality protection behavior, with a turning point at an off-farm income share of approximately 52.5%. Part-time farming initially discourages land protection by reducing agricultural labor input and the scale of land operation, particularly during the early stage of off-farm employment. As the degree of part-time farming increases, however, agricultural socialized services and expanded social networks facilitate the adoption of land protection practices. These effects are more pronounced among farmers who engage in off-farm work for more than six months, operate farmland with a disaster-affected share exceeding 15%, or reside within 20 kilometers of a county town. Among farmers who derive a larger share of their income from rice production, the initial inhibitory effect is weaker and the turning point occurs earlier. The findings suggest that land quality protection policies should account for regional economic conditions, climatic risks, and geographical accessibility. Policy measures should promote agricultural socialized services, encourage appropriately scaled farm operations, develop digital platforms for sharing agricultural information, and strengthen rural infrastructure and disaster prevention systems.

title: How does metaphorical meaning “grow”? – An interpretive approach to literary metaphor from the perspective of Peircean semiotics
abstract: Abstract Traditional metaphor studies mostly focus on conceptual mapping at the cognitive level and tend to regard metaphor as a largely static projection from the source domain to the target domain. Such a perspective fails to fully account for the unique openness of meaning and aesthetic creativity inherent in literary metaphor. To address this limitation, this paper proposes and applies an interpretive framework for literary metaphor based on C. S. Peirce’s triadic theory of signs. The core mechanism of this approach lies in the divergence of sign forms: through the unconventional reconstruction of conventional sign relationships, the fixed connection between signifier and signified is disrupted, thereby driving the dynamic semantic evolution of the interpretant. By analyzing three categories of literary metaphors, this study demonstrates how literary metaphors employ the “interpretive surplus” to break through the closure of conceptual frameworks and facilitate the dynamic “growth” of meaning beyond static conventions. This research argues that literary metaphor is not merely a cognitive tool. Instead, it functions as an aesthetic channel constructed through the interaction among sign, object and interpretant. While maintaining the interpretive openness of texts, literary metaphor realizes the creative generation of meaning and the deepening of aesthetic experience.

title: Deconstructing tourist experiences in China's traditional villages: a cognitive–affective–conative perspective
journal: Journal of Cultural Heritage Management and Sustainable Development
abstract: Purpose While traditional village tourism is rapidly flourishing in China, scholarly research on tourists' experiences within these destinations remains limited. This study explores the tourist experience in China's traditional villages. Design/methodology/approach Using the cognitive–affective–conative model, this study employed a qualitative netnographic approach to investigate tourists' experiences by analyzing online reviews. Findings This study identifies tourism infrastructure, landscape, natural lifestyle, atmosphere, kinaesthesia and education as key dimensions of cognitive experience, while affective experiences encompass enjoyment, nostalgia, social bonding, tension release and negative emotions. Finally, conative experiences are reflected in tourists' intentions to recommend and revisit traditional villages. Research limitations/implications This research highlights the capacity of traditional villages to provide tourists with functional, hedonic, social and emotional value. However, the focus on a single case limits the generalizability of the findings. Future research should examine traditional village tourism across diverse sociocultural contexts. Originality/value Previous research has predominantly examined the protection and sustainable development of traditional villages from suppliers' perspectives. By contrast, this study develops a conceptual framework for understanding tourists' experiences in traditional villages and offers insights into cultural heritage preservation and sustainable tourism development.
